The effects of citrulline malate (CM) on muscle recovery from resistance exercise remains unknown. We aimed to determine if citrulline malate supplementation improves muscle recovery after a single session of high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) in untrained young adult men. Nine young adult men (24.0 ± 3.3 years) participated in a double-blind crossover study in which they received 6 g of CM and placebo (PL) on two occasions, separated by a seven-day washout period. Each occasion consisted of a single session of high-intensity RE (0 h) and three subsequent fatigue tests sessions (at 24, 48, and 72 h) to assess the time course of muscle recovery. During the tests sessions, we assessed the following variables: number of maximum repetitions, electromyographic signal (i.e., root mean square (RMS) and median frequency (MF)), muscle soreness and perceived exertion, as well as blood levels of creatine kinase (CK), lactate, insulin, and testosterone:cortisol ratio. CK levels increased at 24 h post-exercise and remained elevate at 48 and 72 h, with no difference between CM and PL conditions. Muscle soreness increased at 24 h post-exercise, which progressively returned to baseline at 72 h in both conditions. Lactate levels increased immediately post-exercise and remained elevated at 24, 48, and 72 h in both conditions. No significant treatment × time interaction was found for all dependents variables (maximum repetitions, perceived exertion, CK, lactate, RMS, MF, and testosterone:cortisol ratio) during the recovery period. In conclusion, our data indicate that CM supplementation (single 6 g dose pre-workout) does not improve the muscle recovery process following a high-intensity RE session in untrained young adult men. supplementation skeletal muscle weight training amino acids protein exercise 1. Introduction Nutritional supplementation is a common strategy used by athletes and recreationally active adults to improve physical performance and muscle recovery. Nitric oxide (NO)-related supplements have received special attention for their possible ergogenic effects [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. In particular, citrulline malate (CM) has been reported to augment aerobic energy production during exercise and increase phosphocreatine (PCr) during exercise recovery [ 2 ], improve ammonia (NH3) elimination during recovery from exhaustive exercise [ 4 , 5 ], attenuate muscle soreness after high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) [ 6 ], and increase performance during repeated bouts of high-intensity RE [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. CM is formed by combination of L-citrulline (CIT) and malate (or malic acid)—a salt primarily found in apples. The potential ergogenic effects of CM have been attributed to three key mechanisms. First, oral CIT ingestion has been show to increase plasma L-arginine levels [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] at rest and exercise in humans. Given that L-arginine is the main substrate for synthesis of NO, an important modulator of blood flow [ 12 ], it has been suggested that oral CM supplementation may indirectly increase NO synthesis [ 6 ] and thus increase blood flow to active muscles. In this way, CM supplementation could contribute to increase nutrient delivery and/or clearance of waste products [ 13 , 14 ] such as plasma lactate and ammonia, thereby improving muscle function [ 15 ]. Second, CIT is an essential component of the urea cycle in the liver [ 16 ], where L-arginine produced from CIT is catabolized by arginase into ornithine and urea. Given that urea is the major vehicle to eliminate ammonia, a promoter of muscle fatigue via anaerobic glycolysis and consequent lactic acid production [ 17 ], it has been suggested that CIT supplementation may improve ammonia homeostasis [ 18 ] and thus improving muscle function. Third, malate is an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and its greater availability after CM supplementation may augment aerobic ATP production by the TCA cycle through anaplerotic reactions [ 2 ], resulting in decreased muscle fatigue and improved muscle performance [ 2 , 6 , 7 ]. Based on the aforementioned mechanisms, it is postulated that CM supplementation may increase muscle performance and recovery by several ways, including reducing muscle soreness [ 6 ] and fatigue [ 2 ], improving oxygen delivery to the muscle [ 2 ], increasing oxidative ATP production during exercise and increasing PCr during exercise recovery [ 2 ], and lowering lactate and ammonium production [ 19 ]. Despite an abundance of studies on ergogenic effects of CM supplementation, no study to date has examined whether CM supplementation improves recovery of muscle function after high-intensity RE in young adult subjects. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of free CM supplementation on recovery of muscle function after a single session of high-intensity RE in untrained young adult subjects. Based on the physiological properties and beneficial effects of CM on muscle fatigue and performance [ 6 , 7 , 8 ], we hypothesized that free CM supplementation would enhance muscle recovery from RE by improving muscle functional, metabolic, anabolic, and physiological responses.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a single 6g dose of citrulline malate (CM) supplementation on muscle recovery after a high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session in untrained young adult men, examining functional, metabolic, anabolic, and physiological markers. The findings concluded that CM supplementation does not improve the muscle recovery process.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single oral dose of 6 g of citrulline malate (CM) was administered 60 minutes pre-workout, dissolved in 200 mL water. Participants then performed a single session of high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) consisting of 3 sets of 8–12 repetitions at 90% of 10RM for leg press and hack squat exercises, with 2 min rest between sets and exercises, performed with a 1s concentric:2s eccentric cadence. No dose-response comparisons were reported, and no significant treatment × time interaction was found for any measured variables, indicating CM did not improve recovery compared to placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum CK levels increased significantly (p < 0.001) at 24 h post-exercise and remained elevated at 48 and 72 h in both CM and placebo conditions, with no significant difference between treatments (treatment × time p = 0.632).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, released into the bloodstream upon muscle fiber damage, indicating muscle injury and involved in energy transfer.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Blood samples collected pre- and post-exercise, and immediately after muscular fatigue tests (24, 48, and 72 h after RE session) during recovery from a single high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session with CM or placebo supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Metabolic indicator of muscle damage and integrity, commonly used to assess exercise-induced muscle injury and recovery, reflecting impaired muscle function.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma lactate levels increased significantly (p < 0.001) immediately post-exercise and remained elevated at 24, 48, and 72 h in both CM and placebo conditions, with no significant differences between treatments (treatment × time p = 0.456).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis, indicating metabolic stress and fatigue, but also an energy substrate and a waste product associated with lactic acid production.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Blood samples collected pre- and post-exercise, and immediately after muscular fatigue tests (24, 48, and 72 h after RE session) during recovery from a single high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session with CM or placebo supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Metabolic indicator of acute exercise intensity, anaerobic metabolism, and subsequent metabolic recovery; CM supplementation did not show beneficial effects on lactate reduction.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum testosterone: cortisol ratio did not differ between CM and placebo conditions during the recovery period at 24, 48, and 72 h post-exercise (treatment × time p = 0.970; time p = 0.947), indicating no significant treatment × time interaction.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the balance between anabolic (testosterone) and catabolic (cortisol) hormonal states, influencing muscle protein synthesis and breakdown, and serving as an indicator of physiological stress and recovery status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Blood samples collected pre- and post-exercise, and immediately after muscular fatigue tests (24, 48, and 72 h after RE session) during recovery from a single high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session with CM or placebo supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Anabolic indicator commonly used to assess recovery status, potential for muscle adaptation, and risk of overtraining or chronic stress; absence of differences with CM supplementation suggests no effect on muscular regeneration markers.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant treatment × time interaction was found for the number of maximum repetitions during the recovery period, indicating no difference between CM and placebo conditions.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates muscular endurance and resistance to fatigue during repeated efforts.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Assessed during muscular fatigue tests (one set at 100% of 10 RM until failure) in leg press and hack squat exercises, at 24, 48, and 72 h after high-intensity RE sessions.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Assesses the time course of muscle recovery and restoration of muscular endurance capacity.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Perceived intensity (Visual Analog Scale - VAS / OMNI scale)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Perceived intensity of muscle soreness decreased significantly over time (p = 0.004) from 24 h to 72 h post-exercise in both conditions (e.g., CM: 4.2 ± 3.3 cm at 24h to 2.3 ± 2.0 cm at 72h), but with no significant differences between CM and placebo conditions (treatment × time p = 0.819).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: MF slope in the leg press fatigue test did not change significantly over time between CM and placebo conditions (treatment × time p = 0.493; time p = 0.483).
